rw_fill_blanks.title: Antibiotic resistance
rw_fill_blanks.text: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria {{evolve|evolve|evolution|evolved|evolving}} in ways that make medicines less effective. The {{overuse|overuse|shortage|absence|removal}} of antibiotics in both humans and animals has {{accelerated|accelerated|prevented|delayed|stopped}} this process. Unless new treatments are developed, common infections could once again become {{life-threatening|life-threatening|harmless|curable|beneficial}}, a scenario that health authorities describe as one of the greatest {{challenges|challenges|benefits|solutions|achievements}} of the century.

rw_fill_blanks.title: The Silk Road
rw_fill_blanks.text: The Silk Road was not a single road but a vast {{network|network|bridge|river|wall}} of trade routes linking China with the Mediterranean. Merchants rarely travelled its entire length; {{instead|instead|therefore|because|moreover}}, goods passed through many hands along the way. Besides silk, spices and precious stones, the routes {{facilitated|facilitated|prohibited|ignored|reduced}} the exchange of ideas, religions and technologies, {{making|making|made|make|makes}} it one of the most important channels of cultural contact in history.

rw_fill_blanks.title: Urban gardens
rw_fill_blanks.text: Community gardens are becoming increasingly {{popular|popular|popularity|popularly|populate}} in large cities. Apart from providing fresh vegetables, they offer residents a place to {{socialise|socialise|separate|compete|argue}} and learn new skills. Studies have {{shown|shown|showed|shows|showing}} that people who garden regularly report lower stress levels {{than|than|then|that|as}} those who do not.

rw_fill_blanks.title: Coffee's journey
rw_fill_blanks.text: Coffee is thought to have {{originated|originated|invented|ended|grown}} in Ethiopia, where, according to legend, a goat herder noticed his animals became unusually energetic after eating certain berries. By the fifteenth century, coffee was being {{cultivated|cultivated|cultivation|cultivating|culture}} in Yemen, and coffee houses soon became popular {{venues|venues|vehicles|values|versions}} for conversation and debate across the Middle East. When the drink reached Europe, it was initially met with {{suspicion|suspicion|suspicious|suspect|suspend}}, but it quickly won widespread acceptance.

rw_fill_blanks.title: Remote learning
rw_fill_blanks.text: The rapid shift to remote learning exposed significant {{inequalities|inequalities|equalities|qualities|identities}} between students. Those with reliable internet access and a quiet place to study were able to {{adapt|adapt|adopt|adept|admit}} relatively easily, whereas others struggled to keep up. Researchers argue that future education policy must take these differences into {{account|account|amount|access|accident}} if online learning is to {{complement|complement|compliment|complain|compete}} rather than undermine traditional teaching.

rw_fill_blanks.title: Honeybee communication
rw_fill_blanks.text: Honeybees communicate the location of food through a remarkable {{behaviour|behaviour|behave|behaving|behaved}} known as the waggle dance. The angle of the dance {{indicates|indicates|indicate|indicating|indication}} the direction of the food relative to the sun, while its duration signals the {{distance|distance|distant|distinct|instance}}. This system allows a colony to {{exploit|exploit|explode|explore|explain}} new food sources quickly.

rw_fill_blanks.title: City parks
rw_fill_blanks.text: City parks provide residents with space to relax and {{exercise|exercise|exorcise|exercising|exert}}. They also {{reduce|reduce|produce|induce|seduce}} air pollution and help to keep streets cooler during summer. {{Despite|Despite|Although|However|Because}} these benefits, many parks face budget cuts.

mcq_multiple_reading.title: Benefits of bilingualism
mcq_multiple_reading.passage: For much of the twentieth century, raising children with two languages was thought to confuse them and slow their development. Modern research has largely overturned this view. Bilingual children may initially have slightly smaller vocabularies in each individual language, but their total vocabulary across both languages is usually comparable to that of monolingual children. More importantly, regularly switching between languages appears to strengthen executive functions, such as the ability to focus attention and ignore irrelevant information. Some studies have even linked lifelong bilingualism to a delay in the onset of dementia symptoms, although researchers caution that other factors, such as education and lifestyle, may also play a role.
mcq_multiple_reading.question: According to the passage, which of the following are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bilingualism was once believed to harm children's development.
Bilingual children have much larger total vocabularies than monolingual children.
Switching between languages may improve the ability to focus.
Bilingualism has been proven to prevent dementia.
Other factors may contribute to delayed dementia symptoms.

mcq_multiple_reading.title: Desert locusts
mcq_multiple_reading.passage: Desert locusts are usually solitary insects that pose little threat to farmers. However, after periods of heavy rain, when vegetation becomes abundant, their populations can grow rapidly. As the insects are forced into close contact, they undergo a remarkable transformation: they change colour, become more active and begin to move in coordinated groups. A single swarm can contain billions of locusts and travel more than one hundred kilometres in a day, consuming as much food as millions of people. Early warning systems that use satellite data to monitor rainfall and vegetation now allow authorities to treat breeding areas before swarms form.
mcq_multiple_reading.question: Which of the following statements are supported by the passage?

options.text: Locusts are dangerous to crops at all times.
Heavy rainfall can lead to population growth.
Crowding causes changes in locust behaviour and appearance.
Swarms are unable to travel long distances.
Satellite monitoring helps authorities act before swarms develop.

mcq_multiple_reading.title: The Dunning–Kruger effect
mcq_multiple_reading.passage: The Dunning–Kruger effect describes a cognitive bias in which people with limited knowledge or skill in an area tend to overestimate their own ability. In the original 1999 study, participants who scored lowest on tests of logic and grammar rated their performance as well above average. The researchers argued that the skills needed to perform well are often the same skills needed to recognise good performance. Interestingly, the most competent participants slightly underestimated their relative ability, assuming that tasks they found easy must also be easy for others. Later researchers have debated how much of the effect reflects statistical artefacts rather than genuine psychology.
mcq_multiple_reading.question: Which of the following are stated or implied in the passage?

options.text: Low performers tended to overestimate their ability.
The effect was first described in 1999.
Highly competent people overestimated their ability even more.
Recognising good performance requires similar skills to producing it.
All researchers agree the effect is purely psychological.

mcq_multiple_reading.title: Green roofs
mcq_multiple_reading.passage: A green roof is a roof partly or completely covered with plants. Green roofs absorb rainwater, which reduces pressure on city drainage systems, and they provide insulation that lowers heating and cooling costs. They also create habitats for insects and birds. However, they are more expensive to install than conventional roofs and require a structure strong enough to support the extra weight of soil and water.
mcq_multiple_reading.question: According to the passage, what are the benefits of green roofs?

options.text: They absorb rainwater.
They are cheap to install.
They help insulate buildings.
They provide habitats for wildlife.
They make buildings lighter.

paragraphs.text: In 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find that mould had contaminated one of his bacterial cultures.
Around the mould, however, the bacteria had been destroyed, suggesting that it produced a powerful antibacterial substance.
Fleming named this substance penicillin, but he struggled to produce it in large quantities.
It was not until the 1940s that a team in Oxford found a way to mass-produce the drug, saving countless lives during the Second World War.

Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a disease without causing the illness itself.
They do this by introducing a harmless piece or weakened form of the pathogen into the body.
In response, the immune system produces antibodies and memory cells specific to that pathogen.
As a result, if the person is later exposed to the real disease, their body can fight it off quickly.
The first bicycles, built in the early nineteenth century, had no pedals and were pushed along with the feet.
Pedals were later attached to the front wheel, but this design required an enormous wheel to reach a useful speed.
These so-called penny-farthings were fast but dangerous, as riders sat high above the ground.
The invention of the chain drive solved the problem, allowing two equal-sized wheels and a much safer ride.
This 'safety bicycle' quickly became popular and remains the basic design used today.

reading_fill_blanks.title: Glaciers
reading_fill_blanks.text: Glaciers are formed when snow {{accumulates}} over many years and is compressed into ice. Although they appear solid, glaciers slowly {{flow}} downhill under their own weight. Today, most of the world's glaciers are {{retreating}} as global temperatures rise, a trend that threatens the water {{supply}} of millions of people.

reading_fill_blanks.title: Habits
reading_fill_blanks.text: Psychologists explain that a habit consists of three parts: a cue, a routine and a {{reward}}. Over time, the brain begins to {{associate}} the cue with the reward, so the routine becomes almost {{automatic}}.

reading_fill_blanks.title: Volcanic soil
reading_fill_blanks.text: Despite the obvious {{dangers}}, many communities choose to live near active volcanoes. One reason is that volcanic soil is extremely {{fertile}}, as it is rich in minerals released by eruptions. In addition, volcanoes can be a valuable source of geothermal {{energy}} and attract large numbers of {{tourists}}.

reading_fill_blanks.title: Coral bleaching
reading_fill_blanks.text: Coral bleaching occurs when rising water temperatures cause corals to {{expel}} the algae living in their tissues. Without these algae, corals lose their colour and their main {{source}} of food. If temperatures return to normal quickly, corals can {{recover}}, but prolonged heat often leads to their death.

reading_fill_blanks.title: Public speaking
reading_fill_blanks.text: Many people feel {{nervous}} before speaking in public. Experts suggest that careful {{preparation}} and practice in front of friends can greatly increase a speaker's {{confidence}}.

reading_fill_blanks.title: The Industrial Revolution
reading_fill_blanks.text: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late eighteenth century and {{transformed}} the way goods were produced. Machines powered by steam {{replaced}} much manual labour, and people moved in large numbers from the countryside to rapidly growing {{cities}}. Although living standards eventually rose, working conditions in early factories were often {{harsh}}.

mcq_single_reading.title: Placebo effect
mcq_single_reading.passage: The placebo effect refers to an improvement in symptoms that occurs after a patient receives a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill. The effect is thought to arise from the patient's expectations: believing that a treatment will work can trigger real physiological changes, such as the release of natural painkillers in the brain. For this reason, new drugs are tested against placebos in clinical trials, to determine whether their benefits are greater than those produced by expectation alone.
mcq_single_reading.question: Why are new drugs compared with placebos in clinical trials?

options.text: Because placebos are cheaper to produce.
To check whether the drug works better than expectation alone.
To make patients believe they are receiving treatment.
Because placebos contain natural painkillers.

mcq_single_reading.title: Tea in Britain
mcq_single_reading.passage: Although tea is now regarded as a typically British drink, it only became widely popular in the eighteenth century. At first it was an expensive luxury, heavily taxed and enjoyed mainly by the wealthy. Smuggling was common until the government drastically reduced the tax in 1784, after which tea quickly became affordable for ordinary people.
mcq_single_reading.question: What was the main effect of the 1784 tax reduction?

options.text: Tea smuggling increased.
Tea became a luxury for the wealthy.
Tea became affordable for most people.
The government banned tea imports.

mcq_single_reading.title: Urban noise
mcq_single_reading.passage: Noise pollution is often overlooked compared with air or water pollution, yet long-term exposure to traffic noise has been linked to sleep disturbance, stress and even heart disease. The World Health Organization recommends that night-time noise outside bedrooms should not exceed 40 decibels, a level that many city residents regularly experience being exceeded.
mcq_single_reading.question: What is the main point of the passage?

options.text: Air pollution is more harmful than noise pollution.
Noise pollution is a serious but underestimated health risk.
Most cities meet the WHO's night-time noise limit.
Traffic noise only affects people during the day.

mcq_single_reading.title: Typography
mcq_single_reading.passage: Serif typefaces, which have small strokes at the ends of letters, were long considered easier to read in print, while sans-serif fonts were preferred on low-resolution screens. As display technology has improved, however, studies have found little consistent difference in reading speed between the two, suggesting that familiarity and layout matter more than the presence of serifs.
mcq_single_reading.question: What do recent studies suggest?

options.text: Serif fonts are always faster to read.
Sans-serif fonts should only be used in print.
Whether a font has serifs matters less than familiarity and layout.
Low-resolution screens make serif fonts easier to read.
